author: W3C AG WG
title: Audio shifting adjustable
statement: Audio shifting designed to create a perception of motion can be paused or turned off. - content includes audio shifting. - operating system or user agent triggers audio shifting.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Haptic stimulation adjustable
statement: Haptic feedback can be reduced or turned off. - content triggers haptic feedback. - the operating system or user agent converts non-haptic feedback to haptics at user request.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: No flashing over threshold no exceptions
statement: Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds without a minimum size. - Content includes flashes. Avoiding flashing entirely is the safest option because some people who may not know they are susceptible to photosensitive seizures, and some people may have a much larger view of content than the default (zoomed in or with the display close to the eye).
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: No flashing over threshold
statement: Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds. - Content includes flashes. - The flashing is essential. If there is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected. There is research into the size and frequency metrics underway. The exact values are likely to change before WCAG3 is published.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: No visual motion no exceptions
statement: Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: No visual motion
statement: Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds. - The motion or pseudo-motion is essential.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Safe content review
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: We have reviewed content for violent, explicit, or troubling content and provided appropriate warnings before accessing the content. ::assertion-required - title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim) - date of when the review was conducted - date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) Troubling content will vary based on culture or individual situations, and reviews should take target audiences into consideration.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Single flash
statement: Content does not include a change of contrast (over 4.5:1) going from light to dark (or dark to light) of more than 30% of the visible content area (viewport). - A new page/view is loaded. - The flash is essential. This is a new provision for a big, intense, single on/off flash. This is reported as a trigger by group members, but we need data on this, and a definition that includes size/intensity to avoid including non-triggers such as menus. This provision relies on the color contrast algorithm in WCAG 2. When the algorithm is updated for WCAG 3, the contrast metric will also be updated.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Trigger warning available
statement: A warning is provided before users encounter triggers and a mechanism is available to access the same information without the triggering content. - triggers are present. Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Visual stimulation
statement: Visual stimulation from combinations of density, color, movement, etc. can be reduced or turned off.
rationale: Guideline: Users do not experience physical harm from :term[content].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent navigation labels
statement: The labeling of navigation items within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views in the conformance scope or process is consistent. Labels for navigation items that are marked as 'current' within the conformance scope or process. This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
rationale: Guideline: Users have consistent and alternative :term[methods] for navigation.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent navigation order
statement: The relative order of navigation items is consistent within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process. - In a set of pages/views. This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
rationale: Guideline: Users have consistent and alternative :term[methods] for navigation.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent structural order
statement: The relative order of structural components remains consistent throughout each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope. - In a set of pages/views. Relative order means that content can be added or removed, but repeated items are in the same order relative to each other.
rationale: Guideline: Users have consistent and alternative :term[methods] for navigation.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Error messages collocated
statement: Error messages are visually collocated with the error source or the focus is moved to the error message and a mechanism is available to move to the input that is in error. - Error messages relate to user input.
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Error messages persistent
statement: Error messages persist at least until the error is resolved or the user dismisses them.
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Error notifications available
statement: Errors that are programmatically determined are identified and the problem is described to the user in text. - invalid form input - server errors - application errors
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Error suggestions provided
statement: Error messages include suggestions for corrections. - Errors require corrections by the user. - including suggestions would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Errors associated
statement: When input validation fails, the errors are visually and programmatically associated with the element that caused the error or that can resolve it. Failing validation includes but is not limited to: - when input is required and the field is left empty - when the user input does not meet the requested format
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Errors indicated in multiple ways
statement: Error messages are visually indicated using at least two of the following: a symbol that is consistent throughout the conformance scope color that differentiates the error message from surrounding content a textual indication An example of a "textual indication" would be to add "Error: " before the error description.
rationale: Guideline: Users know about and can correct errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Data entry validated
statement: Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either: when the user leaves the field, or when the form is submitted
rationale: Guideline: Users can review, confirm and fix information they submit in order to prevent errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Error prevention review
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: For each form in the conformance claim, we have reviewed the form designs to reduce the possibility of users making mistakes. This review includes checking to make sure that we: Make the user enter as little information as possible. Clearly indicate required fields. For long numbers, divide input fields into chunks (supporting autocomplete across fields). Use an interface where only valid input can be selected. Use autocomplete and personalization of form controls. Use common words and metrics or units that users are likely to be familiar with. Automatically correct input errors when possible and reliable. Provide the user with known suggestions and corrections. ::assertion-required title, role, or organization making the assertion date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) ::assertion-recommended documentation of which forms were reviewed documentation of any changes made as a result of the review date of usability testing, if applicable
rationale: Guideline: Users can review, confirm and fix information they submit in order to prevent errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Errors preventable
statement: Data entry interfaces allow for users to do at least one of the following before submission: Review, confirm, and correct all information. Review and correct input errors found during validation. - entered data is auto-saved and/or reversible. Editors are looking at removing the grey area that may exist in this requirement due to interpretations of the word “submission“ (pressing “Submit” in the UI or receiving information server-side).
rationale: Guideline: Users can review, confirm and fix information they submit in order to prevent errors.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Bidirectional navigation
statement: The keyboard interface can always move forward to the next interactive element and back to the previous interactive element. Although keyboard navigation is required to be bidirectional, it is not required that it be symmetrical, even though this is usually recommended practice. Tabbing through menus, hitting space to open a menu, tabbing off the end of the menu lands you on the next menu. A shift + tab may go back to the last item in the previous menu (symmetrical) or to the last menu (not symmetrical but also does not fail this requirement).
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Custom keys documented
statement: Documentation for each custom keyboard command is actively available on the page/view to which it applies, or within the applicable process.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus movement relevant
statement: Except for skip links and other elements that are hidden but specifically added to aid keyboard navigation, tabbing does not move the keyboard focus onto content that was not visible before the tab action. Accordions, dropdown menus, and ARIA tab panels are examples of expandable content. According to this requirement, these would not expand simply because they include an element in the tab-order contained in them. They would either not expand or would not have any tab-order elements in them. A menu that expands when you tab to it, but then uses arrow keys to navigate in it would pass. But a menu that expands and then requires you to tab through all the newly-visible elements to navigate past it would fail.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus placed
statement: When keyboard focus moves from one context to another within a page/view, whether automatically or by user request, the keyboard focus is preserved so that, when the user returns to the previous context, the keyboard focus is restored to its previous location unless that location no longer exists. When a user closes a modal dialog or other popup, keyboard focus is returned to the element that caused the dialog or popup to open. When there are tags, with a delete button on each tag, the keyboard focus needs to be moved to a meaningful location after a tag is deleted.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus user controlled
statement: The keyboard focus only moves as a result of user interaction. - The keyboard focus automatically moves to the next interactive elements in keyboard navigation order on completion of some user action, such when the focus moves between the fields for a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code. - The keyboard focus results from security or emergency situations, such as warning about an imminent session timeout that would cause the user to lose their work. - The user is informed of the potential keyboard focus move before it happens and given the chance to avoid the move.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Keyboard accessible
statement: All content that can be accessed by other input modalities can be accessed using keyboard interface only. All content includes content made available via mechanisms including but not limited to hovers, right clicks. Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control. The "Keyboard operable" requirement allows you to navigate to all actionable elements, but if the next element is 5 screens down, you also need to be able to access all the content. Also, if the content is in expanding sections, you need to not only open them but also access all of the content, not just its actionable elements.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Keyboard operable
statement: All components on the page/view that can be operated by pointer, audio (voice or other), gesture, camera, or other means can be operated using keyboard interface only.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: No keyboard conflicts
statement: Custom keyboard commands do not conflict with standard platform keyboard commands or they can be remapped.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: No keyboard traps
statement: Components that can be activated or entered using the keyboard interface, can be deactivated or exited using a standard keyboard navigation-operation technique, standard platform keyboard commands. - The non-standard keyboard navigation technique is described in the page/view or earlier in the process. Ensuring that users can exit a modal dialog, menu, or calendar picker after entering it. Ensuring that users can deactivate an animation, video, drop down menu, or carousel after activating it.
rationale: Guideline: Users can navigate and operate :term[content] using only the keyboard.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Keyboard effort comparable
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: - A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that there is minimal difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities. Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control. ::assertion-required - title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim) - date of when the review was conducted - date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) - scope of assertion (if different from the conformance claim) ::assertion-recommended - copy of the review implementing the use of user interface design principles that include minimizing the difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities - whether training was provided for authors - date training was provided - number or proportion of authors who completed the training - copy of the user interface design principles document
rationale: Guideline: Users can use keyboard without unnecessary physical or cognitive effort.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Navigation keys described
statement: If any keyboard action needed to navigate, perceive, and operate the full content of the page/view is not a common keyboard navigation technique, then it is described in the page/view where it is required or on a page/view earlier in the process where it is used. Any platform-related functions are not the responsibility of the author as long as they are not overridden by the content. Examples: - Tab and Shift + Tab to move through elements - Sticky Keys functionality that allows single key activation of multi-key commands
rationale: Guideline: Users can use keyboard without unnecessary physical or cognitive effort.

author: W3C AG WG
title: No repetitive adjacent interactive elements
statement: Adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome are not included in the page/view. - That outcome is a form of dismissal. A common pattern is having a component that includes a linked image and some linked text, where both links go to the same content. Someone using screen reading software can be disoriented from the unnecessary chatter, and a keyboard user has to navigate through more tab stops than should be necessary. Combining adjacent links that go to the same content improves the user experience.
rationale: Guideline: Users can use keyboard without unnecessary physical or cognitive effort.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent pointer cancellation
statement: The method of pointer cancellation is consistent for each type of interaction within a set of pages/views. - It is essential to be different. Where it is essential to be different, it can be helpful to alert the user.
rationale: Guideline: :term[Pointer] input is consistent and all functionality can be done with :term[simple pointer input] in a time and pressure insensitive way.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer activation controllable
statement: At least one of the following is true for functionality that can be activated using a simple pointer input: No down event : The down event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function. Cancel or undo : Completion of the function is on the up event and a mechanism is available to cancel the function before completion, or there is a mechanism to undo the function after completion. Up reversal : The up event reverses any outcome of the preceding down event. - Completing the function on the down event is essential. An example of Cancel would be dragging where there is a pickup action on button down, but it can be canceled by dropping anywhere other than the drop area. Examples of places where action on down event may be essential include a descending-price auction or a game trigger.
rationale: Guideline: :term[Pointer] input is consistent and all functionality can be done with :term[simple pointer input] in a time and pressure insensitive way.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer pressure not relied on
statement: Specific pointer pressure is not the only way of achieving any functionality. - Specific pressure is essential to the functionality. Specific pressure would be essential to a paintbrush feature or advanced signature verification.
rationale: Guideline: :term[Pointer] input is consistent and all functionality can be done with :term[simple pointer input] in a time and pressure insensitive way.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer speed not relied on
statement: Functionality does not rely solely on specific pointer speed. - Specific pointer speed is essential to the functionality. Specific pointer speed would be essential to a paintbrush feature, advanced signature verification, or time-constrained gaming.
rationale: Guideline: :term[Pointer] input is consistent and all functionality can be done with :term[simple pointer input] in a time and pressure insensitive way.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Simple pointer input available
statement: All functionality and content available using complex pointer inputs is also available using a simple pointer input, or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing. Complex pointer inputs include but are not limited to: - double clicks - dragging movements - swipe gestures - multipoint gestures such as pinching, split tap, or two-finger rotor - variable pressure or timing Complex pointer inputs are not banned, but they cannot be the only way to accomplish an action. Simple pointer input is different than single pointer input and is more restrictive than simply using a single pointer.
rationale: Guideline: :term[Pointer] input is consistent and all functionality can be done with :term[simple pointer input] in a time and pressure insensitive way.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Generated speech testing

title: Real time text available

rationale: Guideline: Provide alternatives to speech input and facilitate speech control.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Speech not relied on
statement: Content or functionality does not rely on speech alone. - Speech input is essential to the functionality.
rationale: Guideline: Provide alternatives to speech input and facilitate speech control.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Body movements not relied on
statement: Functionality does not rely solely on full or gross body movement. - Full or gross body movement is essential to the functionality. This includes both detection of body movement and actions to the device, such as shaking, that require body movement.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Eye tracking not relied on
statement: Content and functionality does not rely solely on eye tracking. - Eye tracking is essential. This is primarily aimed at ensuring there is an alternative for people who cannot use eye tracking (but do have sight) due to eye conditions. Some platforms may only allow eye tracking. Ideally the platforms allow additional mechanisms for control.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Hover content persistent
statement: If pointer hover can trigger content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing. - Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent. This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement. Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute. Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Hover or focus content dismissible
statement: A mechanism is available to dismiss content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, unless the additional content does not obscure or replace other content. - Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent. This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement. Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute. Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Hover or focus content persistent
statement: Content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus remains visible until the hover or keyboard focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid. - Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent. This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement. Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute. Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Input method flexible
statement: The ability to switch between input methods is available at any time. This does not mean that all input technologies (pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture) need to be supported, but if an input modality is supported, it is supported everywhere in the content except where a particular input method is essential to the functionality.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Path based gesture not relied on
statement: Path-based gestures are not the only way of achieving any functionality. - A path-based gesture is essential to the functionality.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer accessible
statement: Pointer selection of elements moves the keyboard focus to that element, even if the user selects an interactive element and drags away from the element without activation. - Content can interfere with pointer or keyboard focus behavior. A user scrolls a document down six screens, then clicks on a paragraph with their pointer. The user then presses the Tab key, which moves the focus to the first interactive component after the position on the screen that was clicked, rather than from the previous position, six screens up the document.
rationale: Guideline: Users have the option to use different input techniques and combinations and switch between them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Biometrics not relied on
statement: Biometric identification is not the only way to identify or authenticate. Biometrics includes facial recognition software, fingerprinting, vocal patterns and other voice characteristics.
rationale: Guideline: Users have alternative authentication :term[methods] available to them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Multiple biometrics available
statement: Authentication does not rely solely on a single type of biometrics.
rationale: Guideline: Users have alternative authentication :term[methods] available to them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Voice identification not relied on
statement: Voice identification is not the only way to identify or authenticate.
rationale: Guideline: Users have alternative authentication :term[methods] available to them.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Default focus indicator used
statement: The focusable item uses the user agent default focus indicator.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see which element has :term[keyboard focus].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus indicator contrast sufficient
statement: If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient adjacent contrast and change of contrast. the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see which element has :term[keyboard focus].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus indicator size sufficient
statement: If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient size and adjacency. the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see which element has :term[keyboard focus].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus indicator style guide
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: - Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed. ::assertion-required - title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim) - date of when the design style guide was published - date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) ::assertion-recommended - copy of the policy implementing the use of design style guide on focus style - whether training was provided for authors - date training was provided - number or proportion of authors who completed the training - copy of the design style guide (if any) where focus style has been defined
rationale: Guideline: Users can see which element has :term[keyboard focus].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Default pointer used
statement: The user can ensure that the appearance of the pointer is not overridden by the authored interface. - Changing the pointer appearance is essential.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Enhanced pointer available
statement: Provide a more visible pointer indicator than the platform default. The enhanced pointer indicator can be enabled in a setting, and be visible temporarily (for a few seconds) or permanently.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer activation indicated enhanced
statement: The user can choose to always have a visible pointer indicator. - The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator. This is primarily aimed at eye-tracking and touch-screens, where it is useful for the user to be able to have a visible indicator, but it wouldn't be universal. This aims to avoid it being in the way for some users.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer activation indicated minimum
statement: There is a visible indication of the activation of an interactive element when selected by the pointer. - The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator. This is primarily aimed at touch-interfaces and VR where you don’t have a pointer indicator, but do need to know when something has been selected.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer contrast sufficient
statement: The default pointer meets the @@[non-text-contrast] requirement, and is at least as large as the platform default. the pointer indicator appearance can be adjusted from the platform default. There can be multiple types of pointer indicator. For example, arrow, hand, caret. The size requirement applies to whichever type of indicator would be the default for that scenario.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer focus indicated
statement: There is a visible pointer indicator. - The pointer is on a video - it can be hidden if there is a pointer mechanism to un-hide the pointer indicator. - The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment. Examples of pointers which do not always show the pointer indicator: - A touch-screen interface does not need to have an indicator as the pointer is not on an element before activating it. - An eye-tracking interface highlights the element under the gaze of the user, but otherwise does not have a pointer indicator. - A game where you use the pointer to move the entire view around a virtual environment.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Pointer visible
statement: The pointer indicator is always visible. - The pointer is on a video and is not moving. - The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
rationale: Guideline: Users can see the location of the :term[pointer] focus.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus order meaningful
statement: The keyboard focus moves sequentially through content in an order and way that preserves meaning and operability. - The Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques are considered logical by default. - Having the navigation follow a consistent pattern on the page would be an indication of logic (if it is not consistently random). - A strictly start-to-end order is not required. - Linear means in a single direction (forward/backward) - and is not required as long the non-linear (x-y) technique is in the Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques or is described on the page or where the user will encounter it prior.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine where they are and move through :term[content] (including :term[interactive elements]) in a systematic and meaningful way regardless of input or movement method.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus relevant
statement: The focus order does not include hidden, static, or groups of repeated interactive elements.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine where they are and move through :term[content] (including :term[interactive elements]) in a systematic and meaningful way regardless of input or movement method.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Focus retained
statement: A user can focus on a content "area", such as a modal or popup, then resume their view of all content using a limited number of steps.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine where they are and move through :term[content] (including :term[interactive elements]) in a systematic and meaningful way regardless of input or movement method.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent control location
statement: Where an interactive element with the same purpose is used across pages/views, its visual position in the layout is maintained. - The location changes due to a page variation or viewport change, or - The layout changes due to being part of a process. An e-commerce checkout is an example of where the layout might change within a longer process.
rationale: Guideline: Users can interact with :term[interactive elements] that behave as expected.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Consistent interactions
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: - A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components with the same functionality behave consistently: - Components that perform the same function behave in the same way and use the same visual indicators. - Within the component, interactive elements with the same function have consistent labels. - Standard user interface designs for the platform are used when applicable. ::assertion-required - title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim) - date of when the review was completed - date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) ::assertion-recommended - results from the review - process or policy for maintaining the review
rationale: Guideline: Users can interact with :term[interactive elements] that behave as expected.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Conventional pattern used
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: - A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components follow established conventions: - Each component follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component. - If a component library is used, then each component in the library: - is tested for accessibility before being used - follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component ::assertion-required - title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim) - date of when the review was completed - date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim) ::assertion-recommended - results from the review - process or policy for maintaining the review A component library specifies a set of standardized components used in a product or products. It can include code to use, but at a minimum would define how the component is used and define pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology interactions. Using a component library can help larger teams and organizations provide a consistent experience. Examples of component libraries include GDS, Carbon Design System, and Lion. Examples of platform patterns are ARIA Platform Authoring Guide (web), Apple human interface guidelines, and Android Material Design.
rationale: Guideline: Users can interact with :term[interactive elements] that behave as expected.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Changes to elements notified
statement: Changes to interactive element names, roles, values, or states are visually and programmatically indicated.
rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Interactive element contrast sufficient
statement: Visual information required to identify interactive elements and states meet a minimum contrast ratio test. The interactive element is inactive, or The appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the content author.
rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Interactive element importance indicated
statement: The importance of interactive components is indicated.
rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Interactive element names available
statement: Persistent names (including labels) that identify the purpose of the interactive element are visually and programmatically available. Visible labels can be text or non-text, for instance icons.
rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Interactive elements distinguishable

rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Label included in programmatic name

rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

title: Roles values states properties available

rationale: Guideline: Users have information about :term[interactive elements] that is identifiable and usable visually and using :term[assistive technology].

author: W3C AG WG
title: Conventional layout review
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: We have reviewed layout conventions for similar products or processes. rationale: Guideline: Users have consistent and recognizable layouts available.

author: W3C AG WG
title: All steps listed
statement: A list of all steps in a multi-step process is visually and programmatically available at each step. - The total number of steps is unknown, or the sequence of steps depends on user actions.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Current step indicated
statement: The current step within a multi-step process is visually and programmatically indicated.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Location within product review
statement: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: We have reviewed conventions for presenting current location within the conformance scope. The presentation of current location within the conformance scope uses appropriate visually and programmatically patterns. rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Page view change notified
statement: When content triggers a change of page/view there is a visual change within the view and programmatic notification of the change.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Page view title available
statement: The page/view has a title that describes its name, topic, or purpose. - The technology has no way to include a title.
rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Return to start prominent
statement: Mechanisms that return the user to the starting point of the conformance scope are available in prominent positions both programmatically and visually. rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

rationale: Guideline: Users can determine their location in :term[content] both visually and using assistive technologies.

author: W3C AG WG
title: Numerical metadata available
statement: Numerical information includes sufficient context in written text and a programmatic equivalent to avoid confusion when presenting dates, temperatures, time, and Roman numerals. Numerical metadata is information that provides context about the numbers presented. This context helps users understand what the numbers represent and how they should be read. Without these cues, numbers can be ambiguous or misleading, making it harder for users to understand the intended meaning—especially across different regions, disciplines, or assistive technologies. Dates include markers for day and month such as “3 May 2025” instead of the ambiguous "03/05/2025." Temperatures specify degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit such as "0° C" or "32° F." Times specify am, pm, or 24-hour clock such as "1 pm" or "13:00."
rationale: Guideline: Users can access :term[text content] and its meaning with text-to-speech tools.

title: Layout reflow supported
statement: All content fits within 320 CSS pixels in the default orientation of text without requiring scrolling in more than one direction.
